'''''Pereskia aculeata''''' is a scrambling shrub in the family [[Cactaceae]]. Common names include '''Barbados gooseberry''', '''blade-apple cactus''', '''leaf cactus''', '''rose cactus''', and '''lemonvine'''.<ref>{{citation |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=27356 |title=USDA GRIN Taxonomy |access-date=3 May 2016}}</ref> It is native to [[Tropics|tropical]] [[Americas|America]]. The leaves and fruits are edible, containing high quantities of protein, iron and other nutrients, and it is a popular vegetable in parts of the Brazilian state of [[Minas Gerais]] under the name of {{lang|pt|ora-pro-nóbis}}.

==Description==
Like other members of the genus ''[[Pereskia]]'', these plants are unusual [[cactus|cacti]] with [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|spiny]] non-[[succulent]] [[Plant stem|stems]] and large [[leaf|leaves]].

It is a scrambling [[vine]] growing to {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall in [[tree]]s, with stems {{convert|2|-|3|cm|in|abbr=on}} thick. Younger stems have hooked thorns and older stems have clusters of woody spines. The leaves are {{convert|4|-|11|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.5|-|4|cm|in|abbr=on}} broad, simple, entire, and [[deciduous]] in the [[dry season]]. The strongly scented [[flower]]s are white, cream or pinkish, {{convert|2.5|-|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} diameter, and numerous, produced in [[panicle]]s. The [[fruit]] is a rounded [[Berry (botany)|berry]], translucent white to light yellow, orange, or red, and {{convert|1.5-2|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter. The leaves are edible, containing 20 to 30% of protein in the dry leaf matter. The fruits are also edible, containing numerous small [[seed]]s. It somewhat resembles the [[gooseberry]] in appearance and is of excellent flavor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pereskia aculeata |url=http://www.llifle.com/Encyclopedia/CACTI/Family/Cactaceae/27182/Pereskia_aculeata |access-date=2023-03-14 |website=www.llifle.com}}</ref>

==Distribution==

===Native===
[[South America]], including [[French Guiana]], [[Guyana]], [[Suriname]], [[Venezuela]], [[Brazil]], [[Colombia]], [[Argentina]] and [[Paraguay]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Rojas-Sandoval |first=Julissa |date=2022-01-07 |title=Pereskia aculeata (Barbados gooseberry) |url=http://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/10.1079/cabicompendium.41750 |journal=CABI Compendium |language=en |volume=CABI Compendium |article-number=41750 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.41750 |issn=2958-3969|doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Introduced===
Considered naturalized in the [[United States]], [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], and the [[Caribbean]]. Also introduced to [[China]], [[India]], [[South Africa]], [[Vietnam]], [[Hawaii]], [[Palau]], [[French Polynesia]], and [[Australia]].<ref name=":0" />

==Ecological significance==
A flea-beetle (''[[Phenrica guerini]]''), a leaf-mining moth (''[[Epipagis cambogialis]]''), and a stem-wilter, (''[[Catorhintha schaffneri]])'', feed on the leaves.<ref name=":0" />

Although ''Pereskia aculeata'' is edible and of high nutrition quality, being an alternative to conventional food, this plant is a declared weed in South Africa where it does extensive damage to forest areas by smothering [[indigenous (ecology)|indigenous]] trees. Infestations occur in some [[Forests of KwaZulu-Natal|KwaZulu-Natal forests]] and are embedded in the canopy and difficult to remove. The plant has a tendency to form large, impenetrable clumps and the spines on the stems make control of large infestations difficult. The plants can regrow from leaves or pieces of stem. One specimen that had infested a tree had its stems cut at the base, but after four years the 'dry' stems of the ''Pereskia'' that fell from the tree still set root and regrew.<ref>Purves et al. (1995) {{full citation needed|date=May 2016}}</ref>

==Control==
These plants are extremely difficult to kill and eradicate. It can be controlled by [[triclopyr]], or through [[biological control]] with the flea-beetle  ''Phenrica guerini.'' The flea-beetle has caused significant damage to ''Pereskia'' plants at [[Port Alfred]], [[Eastern Cape]], South Africa, and was also released widely in [[KwaZulu-Natal]], but has not become established there.<ref name="Klein-1999">{{cite journal | title=Biological control of three cactaceous weeds, ''Pereskia aculeata'' Miller, ''Harrisia martinii'' (Labouret) Britton and ''Cereus jamacaru'' De Candolle in South Africa | last=Klein | first=H. | date=1999 | journal=[[African Entomology Memoir]] | number=1 | pages=3–14 | s2cid=55993058}} [[AGRIS]] id [http://agris.fao.org/agris-search/search.do?recordID=ZA2001000773 ZA2001000773]. [[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International|CABI]] [[Invasive Species Compendium|ISC]] [http://www.cabi.org/isc/abstract/19992302942 19992302942] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210512185312/https://www.cabi.org/isc/abstract/19992302942 |date=12 May 2021 }}.</ref>
